guide.summary: The Sustained Investigation (60% of the score) is a body of 15 images showing an inquiry-guided exploration of materials, processes, and ideas over time, with written responses explaining the guiding questions and the practice, experimentation, and revision.

sections.heading: Building an inquiry
sections.body: An inquiry is a question or set of questions that guides your art-making. Strong questions combine an idea and a way of working, for example: 'How can changes in line weight and erasure show memories fading in drawings of my grandmother's kitchen?' Weak questions are too broad ('What is identity?') or too narrow to sustain 15 images ('How do I draw an apple?'). Your questions can evolve; showing how new questions grew from earlier work is evidence of thoughtful investigation.

sections.heading: Practice, experimentation, and revision
sections.body: Readers look for evidence that you developed work over time. Practice means repeated work to build skill; experimentation means trying different materials, processes, compositions, or approaches to the same idea; revision means changing work in response to what you learn through critique or reflection. Include process images such as thumbnails, studies, failed attempts, and details. The sequence of images should tell the story of how your thinking and work changed.

sections.heading: Synthesis and skill
sections.body: The investigation should show synthesis: materials, processes, and ideas working together. Choose media because they serve the idea, not only because they are familiar. Throughout, demonstrate drawing skills: mark-making, line quality, surface manipulation, the illusion of depth and space, light and shade, and composition, using elements and principles of art and design. A range of approaches within a coherent inquiry is a strength; random variety is not.

keyTakeaways: Materials, processes, and ideas should connect.
commonMistakes: Unrelated works grouped under a vague theme.
Questions too broad or too narrow.
Choosing materials without connecting them to ideas.
examTips: Write your question early and revise it as you learn.

practice.prompt: Write a draft response (about 600 characters) identifying the questions that guided your sustained investigation. If you don't have one yet, invent a plausible investigation.

rubric.description: Names a specific idea and approach, not a vague theme.
Shows how the questions shaped choices.
Clear and within the length limit.

practice.sampleResponse: My investigation began with the question: How can changes in line weight and erasure show memories fading in drawings of my grandmother's kitchen? As I worked, I asked how scale and empty space could suggest absence, and whether repeating one image with small changes could show time passing. Later works asked how viewers might complete missing parts themselves.

practice.prompt: Plan the sequence of your 15 images. Describe how the images will show development from first experiments to resolved works.

rubric.description: Each stage connects to the inquiry.
Realistic scope for a school year.

practice.sampleResponse: Images 1–3: thumbnails and quick material tests. Images 4–7: three small studies of the same subject in different media plus one detail, comparing which best serves the idea. Images 8–10: a larger work that failed, its critique-driven revision, and a detail of the revised area. Images 11–15: a resolved series applying what I learned, ending with a piece that raises a new question.

practice.prompt: Write a draft response (about 600 characters) describing how your sustained investigation shows evidence of practice, experimentation, and revision guided by your questions.

rubric.description: Ties changes to the guiding questions.
Gives at least one concrete revision example.

practice.sampleResponse: I practiced layering marks in small daily studies to control value. I experimented with three surfaces (smooth paper, toned paper, sanded board) to see which best showed loss. After critique, I revised image 9 by removing detail at the edges and increasing contrast at the center, which led to the cropped compositions in images 11–15.

practice.prompt: Critique and revise this weak statement: 'My portfolio is about nature. I explored many things and expressed my feelings using different art supplies.'

rubric.description: Identifies vagueness (no question, no specific materials or processes).
Revision names concrete materials, processes, and changes.

practice.sampleResponse:
Weaknesses: it names a broad subject but no question, uses vague verbs (explored, expressed), and never names materials, processes, or how the work changed.

Revision: How can repeated images of one creek over a year show seasonal change? I began with weekly on-site ink sketches, experimented with washes and salt to capture texture, and after critique shifted to large works that crop the water's surface to emphasize movement.
